summary:
Rivers State lies in southern Nigeria and takes its governing law from national instruments; no Rivers-specific statute or enforcement divergence appears in the sources. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, applies in Rivers, as does the Nigerian Criminal Code in the form used across Nigeria's southern states, which criminalises sex between men with penalties up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years.

The SSMPA reaches well beyond marriage. It makes same-sex marriage and civil unions invalid and illegal, criminalises registering, operating, participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations with 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship.

In 2022 a group of Nigerian human rights organisations and activists challenged Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act; the court ruled those provisions unconstitutional and unsecureable nationwide, removing them as a basis for prosecuting LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals. Beyond those struck sections, no legal protections exist for LGBTQ people in Rivers State. Sharia-based states apply penalties from lashing up to death, but Rivers is not one of them.

Police use the Act as a tool of arrest and extortion. Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report documents that arbitrary arrest and extortion by police became commonplace after the Act's passage, including the case of eight of 21 young men arrested but never charged at a birthday party in Ibadan.

Rivers State itself appears in the record as a site of violence against a gay visitor. Human Rights Watch records that Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos, travelled to Port Harcourt in January 2015 to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook and was attacked and sexually abused there; he did not report the assault to police.

Official foreign guidance warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. Dating applications carry an entrapment risk nationwide: 'kito' gangs lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Care access is chilled by the same arrest and extortion risk. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement across Nigeria takes the form of mass arrests at social venues, a pattern a visitor to Rivers should expect to be replicated locally: 100-plus party-goers arrested at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018; 57 young men at Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. These are raw counts reported by the source, not per-capita rates, and they track where raids occurred rather than comparative state danger.

A decade-outcome assessment by Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (August 2024) finds the 2014 Act has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and increased attacks since it passed.

Police have stopped and beaten people for appearance alone. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'.

Trans-specific violence has drawn official misgendering and impunity: the beaten body of the 33-year-old trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama' was found on an Abuja highway in August 2024, with police describing 'a man fully dressed in female clothing'; by February 2025 no suspects had been charged.

Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) served a six-month Naira-abuse sentence in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, from 12 April to 5 August 2024; an October 2024 panel found her placement in a maximum-security facility violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act for a first-time offender, leaving trans prison placement discretionary.

Rivers State residents live under the same national framework as visitors, with no local protective instrument: the Nigerian Criminal Code applicable in the south and the SSMPA 2014 both bind, and no legal protections exist for LGBTQ people.

Human Rights Watch records that after the Act's passage, arbitrary arrest and extortion by police became commonplace, a pattern affecting residents in their daily movement and associations.

LGBTQ Nigerians report that the Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work; many fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes to police.

Residents face 'kito' gang entrapment through dating applications, with victims beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Rivers State has issued any executive or police directive on enforcement of the SSMPA, or any divergence from other southern states, is not sourced in the inventory.

The 2022 court ruling striking Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) is reported as nationwide in effect, but the inventory does not identify the court, the case name, or any appeal status; that remains unresolved.

No Rivers-specific incident of mass arrest, venue closure or police raid appears in the inventory; the enforcement examples cited are from other states and are offered as pattern evidence only.

Whether the proposed cross-dressing criminalisation reported by Reuters in September 2022 has since been enacted is not sourced here.
